name: Karl Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior researcher at the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, parties or government. Your answers are confidential. What happens on a usual workday?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 27 and lead the tax review team at Rowan & Pike, an accounting firm with many small business clients. I have a master's degree and a chartered accountancy qualification, and I'm one of the strongest at finding a filing error before it reaches a client. The pay is high for my job, but I earn it during the weeks when late records arrive in heaps.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me about home, your savings and how you use new tools.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my partner, Inez, who works as a paramedic, and we have no children. I have nine months of expenses saved, and there are plenty of accounting firms around here if I needed another post. I use AI now and then to draft a client explanation after another accountant has tried it; I verify every tax rule. I favour stronger worker voice and public rules for powerful software, but I want evidence before a new tool touches client files.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau — Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team that a small time saving is useful if we can explain every return we sign. I would want clients to know when a routine draft came from software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My pay and nine months of savings leave me in a good position if little changes. I do worry the partners might turn ten saved minutes into another target without asking the team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep reviewing tax returns and marking any AI-assisted draft for a second human check. In the first year I'd take the current plan to the staff association and ask for clear disclosure to clients, without calling it a crisis.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about my own income. There is room to settle a small software rule while work carries on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would that disclosure say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A short line in the client letter saying which part was drafted by software and who checked it. I would not put a machine's name where a responsible accountant should be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you expect the partners to accept it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know; I'd ask at the next staff meeting. There are enough firms nearby that I can speak plainly without risking next month's rent.

say: I would tell clients when **software drafts** part of a letter.
I would keep a **named accountant** responsible for every return.
think: My **income is secure** with high pay and nine months saved.
I worry modest time savings could become **higher targets**.
do: Keep checking **tax returns** and marking AI drafts for human review.
Raise **client disclosure** at the next staff association meeting.
feel: He feels **calm** about income while wanting clear software rules.
S0.quote: I would not put a machine's name where a responsible accountant should be.
fieldNote: His **strong cushion** lets him raise a workplace rule without fearing next month’s rent.
He sees mild AI mainly as a **disclosure question**, with human review already part of his routine.

steps.text: Keep reviewing Rowan and Pike returns and marking AI-assisted drafts
Raise client disclosure at next staff association meeting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption — Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the team deserves paid training and notice before the firm changes review targets. If software writes and checks returns, a partner still has to answer for the final number.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A lot of my work is checking and writing, so I expect fewer new accounting posts even if my own senior role stays. Our office could grow fees with faster work and still let the junior pipeline dry up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the staff association to request a written staffing plan and paid training hours, then test a proven review tool on twenty closed files with the firm's permission. In the first year of change, I'd track mistakes and ask for a meeting if the partners stop filling junior vacancies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the people entering the trade. My salary is likely safe for now, but the next accountant needs a first rung.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you bring to that meeting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show the list of twenty files and the errors the tool missed. The next accountant needs a first rung. The association could ask the partners to keep one trainee post open if the work still supports it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the firm refuses the trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not put live client data into a tool on my own. I'd stay with the existing review system and check which local firms offer paid training before considering a move.

say: I would ask for **paid training** before new review targets.
I would defend a **trainee place** if faster work still funds one.
think: My **senior wage** probably holds, though routine desk work shrinks.
I fear a lost **junior pipeline** more than immediate dismissal.
do: Request a **written staffing plan** through the staff association.
Test **twenty closed files** with firm permission and paid training.
Track **missed errors** before accepting a higher review target.
feel: He feels **uneasy** because his wage looks safe while entry jobs may shrink.
S1.quote: The next accountant needs a first rung.
fieldNote: He uses the **staff association** for a specific staffing and training request.
He will test only **closed files** with permission and paid time, then use errors as evidence.

steps.text: Ask staff association for written staffing and paid training plan
Test twenty closed files during paid firm-approved training
Track missed tax errors before accepting higher review targets

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028 — Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Rowan & Pike staff that thinking AGI in 2028 would change the fee for almost every return. We need a record of the firm's plans and a public rule on who signs a machine-prepared filing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My desk work meets AGI in 2028; robots around 2031 do not delay that. I might keep a senior review post, but the partners may cut the team sharply, and even my high salary could go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd keep nine months of bills in cash, add another hundred a month from my high salary and join the association's request for a dated consultation on staffing. In the first year after 2028, if my paid hours are cut, I'd apply for advertised salaried tax oversight posts at nearby firms and use the reserve while I search; I would not assume a vacancy exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about my own wage now. Nine months of savings won't restore the fees that pay my accountant's salary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the association to demand?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A month of notice before any staff cut, paid retraining for remaining reviewers and a named person on every tax return. I would join the delegation, not just sign a note.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Inez say about the reserve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Inez, my partner, says her paramedic shifts are steady for now, but the rent should not depend on one income. We agreed the reserve stays for bills, not a business launch.

say: I would demand a **dated staffing consultation** before cuts.
I would seek a **named signer** on machine-prepared tax filings.
think: My **high-paid desk role** could still be cut in 2028.
The **2031 robot date** gives tax thinking work no protection.
do: Add **one hundred monthly** to my nine-month cash reserve.
Apply for **advertised paid oversight** posts if my hours fall after AGI.
feel: He feels **anxious** because his own high wage could disappear.
S2.quote: Nine months of savings won't restore the fees that pay my accountant's salary.
fieldNote: He moves from concern for juniors to **his own wage** when AGI reaches desk work in 2028.
His association request specifies **notice and paid training** rather than a general call for fairness.

steps.text: Add one hundred monthly to nine-month emergency reserve
Join staff association delegation seeking notice and paid training
Apply for advertised salaried tax oversight posts if paid hours fall after 2028

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031 — Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years allows a proper plan for staff and clients, with the partnership and workers at the same table. A quick email the week before launch would not be enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could build an even bigger reserve by 2031, but I would be 32 and still need a career. Full AGI can do the tax reasoning I sell. My senior title cannot protect the tax reasoning I sell from AGI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the staff association to negotiate paid training in tax dispute mediation next year, if the firm can offer real casework. I would also set aside two hundred a month; in the first year after 2031, if my review salary falls, I'd apply for posted salaried regulator or college finance roles and take only funded mediation hours while searching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious, though the time makes a job search less rushed. I want a path for colleagues who don't have nine months saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why mediation when AGI can reason too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A client in a dispute may still want a person who can explain and represent them, though I can't promise that fee survives. I'd test it on actual paid cases before paying for a qualification.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would help colleagues without savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The association should ask for paid study hours and notice of vacancies before anyone loses a cheque. I would put that in the written proposal, not just speak for myself.

say: I would ask for **paid mediation practice** on real cases.
I would make **vacancy notice** part of the staff proposal.
think: At **32 in 2031**, I will still need a long paid career.
My **seniority** cannot guarantee tax reasoning remains valuable.
do: Negotiate **paid dispute practice** through the staff association next year.
Save **two hundred monthly** while my salary continues.
Seek **posted salaried finance roles** if my pay falls after 2031; take only funded mediation hours while searching.
feel: He feels **anxious**, but has time to prepare and support colleagues.
S3.quote: My senior title cannot protect the tax reasoning I sell from AGI.
fieldNote: He ties training to **real paid cases** and doubts whether clients will keep paying for mediation.
His concern for colleagues without savings produces a **written request** for paid study and vacancy notice.

steps.text: Ask staff association to negotiate paid dispute practice and vacancy notice

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036 — Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the partners a decade is enough to let staff shape a fair transition and let clients test a new service. I would not promise every current post lasts to 2036.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 37 I would still need to earn, but ten years and nearby firms would make me less frightened. My thinking work changes in 2036, while Inez's hands-on paramedic work faces robots around 2039; both dates belong in our budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put three hundred a month into our joint long-term fund and ask for a paid trial of tax-dispute representation at Rowan & Pike, with fees going to the firm. In the first year after 2036, if clients still pay enough to fund my salary, I'd stay; if not, I'd apply for posted salaried finance roles nearby and use the fund for rent during the search.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy rather than frightened. A decade gives us time to prove what clients will pay for and to save for a gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How will you judge the trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd count second-year renewals and whether fees cover the hours of the people doing the work. A tax-dispute trial that only works because staff work unpaid evenings has failed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you campaign for a rule beyond your firm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I'd join the association's letter asking the regulator to require a named human signer on tax returns made with AGI. I would write the section on how our review checks work.

say: I would seek a **paid firm trial** of dispute representation.
I would ask the regulator for a **named human signer**.
think: At **37 in 2036**, I still need work, though nearby firms offer choices.
Inez’s **2039 robot risk** means our joint fund matters too.
do: Save **three hundred monthly** into our joint reserve.
Run a **paid dispute trial** with firm approval and fees to the firm.
Apply for **posted finance roles** if client fees cannot fund my salary after 2036.
feel: He feels **uneasy**, with a decade to test fees and save.
S4.quote: A tax-dispute trial that only works because staff work unpaid evenings has failed.
fieldNote: He tests a firm service against **paid staff hours** and renewal, rejecting an unpaid workload.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because my review salary could fall before the team or clients know the rules. I would want a dated staffing consultation, paid training and real posted oversight jobs. My savings help me speak up, but they do not pay my colleagues' rent.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who gets the benefit when one accountant can finish ten returns in an afternoon. The partners can buy software overnight; a good tax reviewer still takes years to grow.

headlineQuote: The partners can buy software overnight; a good tax reviewer still takes years to grow.
portrait: Karl, **27**, leads tax review at Rowan & Pike with a master’s degree and chartered qualification.
He earns **high pay**, has nine months saved, lives with paramedic Inez and has many nearby accounting firms.
He uses AI **occasionally** after colleagues test it, and seeks worker input and clear client disclosure.
He feels secure in a plateau, then fears **2028 salary cuts** while using the association to seek paid training.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could cut his review salary before the firm agrees on staffing and client rules.
whatWouldHelp: A **dated consultation**, paid training and posted salaried oversight roles would give workers practical options.
